lesson.title: The Craft, and the Limits, of Predicting What Comes Next
lesson.summary: Technology forecasting is the discipline of predicting how technologies will develop and spread, and a look at why even careful, expert forecasts routinely miss.
lesson.body:
Technology forecasting is the general discipline of trying to predict how a technology will develop and spread: its capability trajectory, its timeline, its eventual adoption rate. It long predates Gartner's specific hype cycle model and spans corporate strategy, government research funding decisions at agencies like DARPA, academic technology management research, and financial and popular journalism.

A few real methods are worth knowing. Trend extrapolation fits a curve, often exponential or S shaped, to historical data, the way Moore's Law has been extrapolated for semiconductors, and projects it forward. Expert elicitation surveys specialists directly, sometimes structured as a Delphi method where experts anonymously revise their estimates across multiple rounds in an attempt to converge. Patent and publication analysis, sometimes called bibliometrics, treats research output as a leading indicator of where a field is heading. Scenario planning, used heavily and famously by organizations like Royal Dutch Shell, builds multiple plausible futures rather than committing to one point forecast.

Forecasting is hard for structural reasons, not because forecasters are careless. Technology growth is typically S shaped, slow at first, steep in the middle, saturating at the end, rather than exponential forever, but nobody knows in advance exactly where the inflection points sit. Breakthroughs are also inherently discontinuous: if a forecaster could reliably predict exactly when a specific breakthrough would occur, that breakthrough would, in a meaningful sense, have already happened.

A second structural difficulty is complementary technologies. A core invention's real world usefulness usually depends on several other things maturing at the same time, supporting infrastructure, the falling cost of complementary components, regulation, and business model innovation, and forecasters routinely underweight whichever of those dependencies happens to be slowest. This connects directly to Technology Adoption Curves: a technology can be scientifically complete and still sit in limbo for years waiting on its slowest moving complement.

Nuclear fusion power offers a clean, safely documented illustration. Researchers and journalists have, at various points across roughly seven decades of fusion research, described commercially viable fusion power as still about thirty years away, a pattern well known enough inside the field that it has become something of a running joke among fusion scientists themselves. The pattern is instructive precisely because these were expert forecasters working in good faith on a real research program, and they still consistently underestimated the remaining distance, not from a lack of qualification but because the remaining problems were disproportionately the boring, hard to forecast parts: materials, containment, and cost, rather than the initial breakthrough physics.

Because forecasting carries these structural weaknesses, the sensible response is not to trust any single point prediction at face value, but to track base rates, how often forecasts like this one have panned out historically, and track records, how a given forecaster or field has done before. Those are exactly the tools the next two chapters build.
